newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rifkind rebuts Kohl, sees EU unity danger.
newsitem.headline: Rifkind rebuts Kohl, sees EU unity danger.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Wednesday Chancellor Helmut Kohl was wrong on European Union integration and suggested the veteran German leader was out of touch with popular opinion.

Rifkind, on a visit to stir up a critical debate about Europe in one of the EU's most pro-European states, said many members were unclear whether they wanted a United States of Europe or the community of nation states as Britain preferred.

Earlier on Wednesday, Rifkind told BBC radio the British government was basically hostile to the planned economic and monetary union (EMU) and told the Bild daily in Germany he did not think it would start on schedule in 1999.
Rifkind said in Bonn he did not agree with Kohl that further integration of the European Union was an issue of war and peace and the bloc had to move forward or it would stumble.
"I don't myself believe his analysis is correct," he said. "The new Europe is not the Europe of the 19th century. The nation state today is not the nation state of the past."
He stressed at a news conference that European leaders must not lose touch with "what ordinary people in Britain or France or Germany or Italy are thinking and talking and saying".

Without naming Kohl, he criticised politicians who focus on "great European structures" and had unclear ideas about how far integration should go. "Sometimes such efforts lose contact with the aspirations and concerns of our respective peoples. Opinion polls in Germany sometimes indicate high levels of concern about various aspects of integration."

Rifkind, whose one-day visit was part of a tour aimed at speaking directly to European voters, was later due to address a think tank linked to Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and ask how far Kohl wanted to go towards a united Europe.
"How far does a United States of Europe differ from the proposals made by Germany and others for ever closer integration?" he asked, according to an advance text.

He said the German view of a more integrated union "looks like an agenda for creating a European state" and criticised Bonn's support for more EU majority voting as a potential threat to democracy itself.

"It is no good saying that the convoy must not go at the pace of its slowest ship," he said, echoing a common German argument in favour of majority voting. "We are not talking about convoys, we are talking about democracy."
